CYTOGENETICS LABORATORY
GENOMIC MICROARRAY ANALYSIS REPORT

PATIENT INFORMATION
Patient: [redacted name]
DOB: [redacted date]
Sex: Male
MRN: [redacted ID]
Specimen Type: Peripheral blood
Collection Date: [redacted date]
Received Date: [redacted date]
Report Date: [redacted date]

CLINICAL INDICATION
Infant requiring chromosomal analysis based on clinical presentation

TEST PERFORMED
Oligonucleotide Array Comparative Genomic Hybridization (Array CGH)

METHODOLOGY
Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood and analyzed using oligonucleotide array CGH. The array platform utilized was GeneScan 8500 containing approximately 60,000 genome-wide probes with a median resolution of 120kb. Data analysis was performed using GenomeView software. All genomic coordinates are based on the GRCh37/hg19 reference genome assembly.

RESULT: ABNORMAL

arr[GRCh37] 11p15.4p14.1(4,209,322-28,368,511)x3

A 24.159 Mb duplication was detected on the short arm of chromosome 11, spanning from band p15.4 to p14.1 (genomic coordinates: 4,209,322-28,368,511). This duplicated region contains approximately 100 genes. No other clinically significant copy number imbalances were detected. The array analysis confirmed a male chromosome complement (XY).

INTERPRETATION
The 24.159 Mb duplication of 11p15.4-p14.1 represents a significant genomic imbalance that is likely causative of the patient's clinical features. Previous cases reported in the medical literature with similar duplications involving this chromosomal region have been associated with hypotonia and facial dysmorphism, consistent with the clinical presentation in this patient.

This duplication results in three copies (trisomy) of all genes within the affected region. The large size of this duplication and the number of dosage-sensitive genes involved support its pathogenic classification.

If this duplication is present in a balanced form in either parent, there would be a 50% risk of transmission to offspring. De novo duplications carry a low recurrence risk for future pregnancies.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Blood samples are needed from both the patient and parents for parental array CGH studies to determine if this duplication is inherited or de novo.
2. Clinical genetics consultation is recommended to correlate these findings with the patient's phenotype.
3. Genetic counseling is strongly recommended when the patient reaches reproductive age to discuss the 50% risk of transmission to offspring and available reproductive options.
4. Consider additional clinical evaluations based on genes within the duplicated region.

LIMITATIONS
This array CGH analysis will not detect balanced chromosomal rearrangements, low-level mosaicism (<20%), point mutations, or copy number variants smaller than the resolution of this array.

Reported by: [redacted name], PhD, FACMG
Laboratory Director: [redacted name], MD, PhD
